title: Minimally Invasive Surgery and Emerging Technologies in Emergency Abdominal Surgery: A Narrative Review Focusing on Indocyanine Green Fluorescence, Robotic Assistance and Artificial Intelligence
content: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is progressively transforming emergency abdominal care through high-definition visualization, indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence imaging, robotic-assisted platforms and the emerging integration of artificial intelligence (AI). This narrative review traces the evolution from conventional laparoscopy to fluorescence-guided, robotic-assisted and AI-supported emergency surgery. Publications were identified in PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science, prioritizing guidelines, consensus statements, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and recent clinical studies. Current evidence supports a laparoscopic-first approach in hemodynamically stable patients with acute appendicitis, acute calculous cholecystitis, perforated peptic ulcer and selected cases of adhesive small bowel obstruction, strangulated hernia, complicated diverticulitis and penetrating trauma, whereas open laparotomy remains mandatory in hemorrhagic or septic shock. Near-infrared ICG imaging has expanded from elective to emergency practice for biliary anatomy identification, bowel perfusion assessment and anastomotic decision-making, although prospective emergency data remain limited. Robotic systems offer dexterity, ergonomics and integrated imaging, but emergency use is constrained by availability, cost, docking time and team training. AI is being explored for anatomy recognition, risk prediction, augmented reality and autonomous subtasks, with decision support the most realistic near-term role. The value of these technologies depends less on the technology itself than on patient selection, surgical expertise, team preparedness and institutional readiness.
